attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter, stated in his own voice.

semantics.note: An unqualified 'will' forecast that each lab loses tens of billions in 2026 and more in 2027. Leaving out the compute-buyer assertion is acceptable because it is a separate claim.

contract.note: Calendar years and a floor of at least $20B for 'tens of billions' are ordinary readings. The net-loss metric is debatable, since Anthropic's losses are mostly fair-value changes, but it does not matter while the forecast is not yet due.

evidence.note: Anthropic S-1 shows an unaudited H1 2026 net loss of $80.7B, mostly fair-value changes. This is interim data and says nothing about the full year or 2027.
A January 2026 secondary report of an OpenAI internal projection of about $14B in 2026 losses. It is a projection, not a realized result, and its accounting basis is unclear.

reviews.rationale: The forecast runs to the end of 2027, after the evaluation date. Neither company has final 2026 annual results, so the early-resolution rule is not met. Interim losses and projections cannot settle full-year net losses, so the claim is unresolved for now.

attribution.note: Zitron's own analytical statement in his newsletter.

semantics.note: The 'Assuming… intends to pay' antecedent is kept, though the draft turns intent into 'is to pay' and drops 'reported'. 'Will have to' is a firm claim of necessity through 2030.

contract.note: Reading 'raise' as external financing and 'hundreds of billions' as at least $200B is ordinary. Marking the condition as met rests only on a press report of projected spending, which is a weak basis for intent, but this does not matter before the deadline.

evidence.note: WSJ-sourced report of about $750B in projected compute spending through 2030. It bears on the antecedent only, not on the financing or demand outcome.

reviews.rationale: The horizon runs to 2030, and no records of completed payments, annual financing or utilization exist yet. The packet only shows the reported spending plan, which goes to the antecedent. The forecast is not due, so it stays unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion in his newsletter.

semantics.note: Excluding lab-derived demand follows from the preceding sentence. The Jane Street and NVIDIA exceptions and the 'warrant all this capex' qualifier are kept.

contract.note: Not exempting Meta is fair, because this sentence does not exempt it. Still, 'significant' and 'warrant all this capex' have no threshold or capex denominator, so the result depends on interpretation.

evidence.note: CoreWeave's roughly $21B Meta deal through 2032, a company disclosure. It cuts against the claim of no significant independent customers, but no capex comparison is available.
Nebius-Meta deal: $12B of dedicated capacity plus up to $15B conditional. It cuts against the claim, but it predates the quarter and its link to capex adequacy is not established.

reviews.rationale: Meta's large CoreWeave and Nebius commitments are a significant customer the speaker did not except, and they cast real doubt on the claim. But the contract requires showing these commitments support a material portion of the relevant neocloud capex, and the packet has no capex totals. The contradiction condition is not shown, so the claim is unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion in his newsletter.

semantics.note: A causal claim that the growth trajectories depend on the labs' financing and demand. All the named companies and the 'every other neocloud' scope are preserved.

contract.note: Reading 'contingent' as material dependence of expected growth is an ordinary reading, and the contract rightly refuses to infer the whole neocloud class from CoreWeave alone.

evidence.note: CoreWeave's Meta deal shows demand beyond the labs for one neocloud. It does not show whether growth could be sustained without the labs.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no company-level growth sensitivity analysis and no attributable analyst models across Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Oracle or the neoclouds. A single CoreWeave-Meta contract qualifies the claim's scope but cannot establish or refute the claimed dependency, so the claim is unresolved.
